title: Parse a JSON Pointer String
background:
JSON Pointer values are usually received as text from configuration, API input, or document metadata. The first practical step in most workflows is turning that text into a `JsonPointer` value you can pass to evaluation or composition APIs.

In this lesson, you will parse incoming pointer text and inspect a simple property (`SegmentCount`) to confirm the pointer was constructed correctly. This establishes the parse-first workflow used throughout the rest of the pointer lessons.

title: Parse Safely with TryParse
background:
`JsonPointer.Parse(...)` is the direct path when input is trusted, but user-supplied pointers are often invalid. In those scenarios, exception-driven control flow creates noisy code and makes input validation harder to read.

`JsonPointer.TryParse(...)` lets you validate and parse in one step while keeping branching explicit. This lesson focuses on using that safe parse workflow and returning structured output that reflects parse success.

title: Evaluate on JsonNode
background:
When your application already uses `JsonNode`, the most direct pointer workflow is `TryEvaluate(JsonNode?, out JsonNode?)`. This API returns whether the path was found and exposes the matched node separately.

In this lesson, the pointer and document are provided. Your task is to call `TryEvaluate` and return the matched value when available.
instructions: Use `TryEvaluate(...)` to set `found` and `value`, then return `value` only when `found` is true.

title: Distinguish Missing Path vs Found Null (JsonNode)
background:
With `JsonNode`, a missing path and a found JSON `null` both involve null-like values, but they are not the same outcome. `TryEvaluate(...)` separates these cases through its `bool` return and `out` node result.

That distinction is important when business logic treats absent data differently from explicit null values. This lesson focuses on preserving that information in the returned shape.
instructions: Call `TryEvaluate(...)` and return `{ found, value }` so missing and null results remain distinguishable.

title: Evaluate on JsonElement
background:
Many code paths process JSON through `JsonDocument` and `JsonElement` for lower allocation overhead and immutability. `JsonPointer.Evaluate(JsonElement)` supports this workflow directly and returns a nullable `JsonElement`.

In this lesson, you will evaluate a pointer against a `JsonElement` document and return the matched value as `JsonNode` for test comparison.
instructions: Use `Evaluate(JsonElement)` to set `result`, then return it as JSON when found.

title: Distinguish Missing Path vs Found Null (JsonElement)
background:
`Evaluate(JsonElement)` returns `JsonElement?`, so a missing path appears as a null nullable value. A found JSON `null` is different: it is a present `JsonElement` whose `ValueKind` is `Null`.

When your application distinguishes absent data from explicit nulls, that difference must be preserved. This lesson focuses on returning both presence and null-kind information.
instructions: Evaluate the pointer, then return `{ found, isJsonNull, value }` using `JsonElement?` semantics.
